h1: Contract manufacturing for drinks brands: beer, wine and spirits
title: Contract Manufacturing for Drinks Brands | Craft Beer School
desc: How contract manufacturing works for beer, wine and spirits brands: who does what, the risks on both sides and what an agreement should cover.
teaser: Contract production lets a brand sell before it owns a plant. It also hands part of your product to someone else.
standfirst: Contract manufacturing means one company makes a drink for another's brand. This guide explains how it works for beer, wine and spirits and what to settle before you start.
sections:
A brand owner has the recipe, the name and the customers. A host plant has the equipment, the people and spare capacity. The host brews, ferments or distils and packs the product. The brand sells it.

Brands use this route to test a market without building a plant. Plants use it to fill idle capacity. Done well, both benefit. Done badly, both lose money and the brand loses a reputation.

Beer is the easiest to contract because the process is repeatable and brewing is quick. A brand can often move a recipe to a host brewery once the host has the right equipment.

Wine depends on the harvest. Contracts often cover grapes, fermentation and ageing over months, so timing and quality control need to be agreed from the start.

Spirits add excise control and, for aged products, years of maturation. The host's licences, warehouses and records matter as much as its equipment. In India, alcohol is a state subject, so each state treats contract arrangements in its own way and rules change. Check with a licensing adviser or lawyer before you sign.

• The specification: recipe, raw materials, process steps, quality limits and packaging
  • Ownership of the recipe, the brand and any process improvements
  • Quality checks, sampling, rejection rights and who bears the cost of a failed batch
  • Pricing method, minimum volumes and how capacity is booked
  • Raw material purchasing, stock holding and wastage
  • Licences and compliance: who holds which licence and who answers to the authority
  • Confidentiality, audit rights and termination

Put the specification in writing before the first batch. Disputes almost always come back to a spec that was vague.

The brand depends on a host it does not control. Beer that comes out slightly different will be blamed on the brand, not the host. Insist on agreed tests, regular tasting against a reference sample and the right to inspect.

Read our guide on mistakes in project reports before you commit. Underestimated costs and overestimated volumes hurt contract arrangements as much as new plants.

A host takes on a brand's quality promise. It also takes on cash risk if the brand orders less than agreed or pays late. Minimum volumes, payment terms and raw material commitments protect the host.

Hosts should also guard their own process. A contract batch that disrupts the plant's own beer schedule costs more than it earns.

We set up contract manufacturing arrangements for drinks brands and plants. That covers the choice of host, the technical specification, the trial batches and the agreement terms. For an existing arrangement we can review quality and costs from both sides. Work runs remotely by video call and shared data, with site visits by arrangement.

We do not name clients or quote results in advance. Our guide on business health reports shows how a plant can check whether contract work is paying its way.

Visit the plant if you can, or ask for a video walk-through. Look at cleanliness, laboratory equipment, record keeping and how they handle their own product. A host that cannot show you a batch record for its own beer will not produce one for yours.

Ask about capacity honestly. A plant that is busy in summer may have room in winter, which suits a seasonal brand. Ask what happens if their equipment fails mid-contract.

Run a small trial batch before signing a long agreement. Taste it against your reference and measure it against your specification. A trial costs little next to a failed first order.

Finally, meet the people who will run your batches. A good working relationship with the host's brewer or winemaker solves more problems than any clause in the contract.

Keep a reference sample from every batch. If a customer complains six months later, you can taste what left the plant instead of arguing about it. Write the storage conditions and shelf life into the agreement as well, so both sides know how long a sample must be kept.
faqs: Can a new brand start with contract production?
Yes. Many brands do. You need a clear specification, a host with the right equipment and licences and an agreement that covers quality and volumes.
The agreement should say. Most brand owners keep the recipe and require confidentiality. Settle this before sharing details.
Is contract manufacturing legal for alcohol in India?
Arrangements depend on state rules, which differ and change. Speak with a licensing adviser or lawyer in the state where production will take place.
